arXiv:2510.12795v1 [cs.CV] 14 Oct 2025

CuMPerLay: Learning Cubical Multiparameter Persistence Vectorizations

Caner Korkmaz1   Brighton Nuwagira2   Barış Coşkunuzer2   Tolga Birdal1

1 Imperial College London   2 UT Dallas
Abstract

We present CuMPerLay, a novel differentiable vectorization layer that enables the integration of Cubical Multiparameter Persistence (CMP) into deep learning pipelines. While CMP presents a natural and powerful way to topologically work with images, its use is hindered by the complexity of multifiltration structures as well as the vectorization of CMP. In face of these challenges, we introduce a new algorithm for vectorizing MP homologies of cubical complexes. Our CuMPerLay decomposes the CMP into a combination of individual, learnable single-parameter persistence, where the bifiltration functions are jointly learned. Thanks to the differentiability, its robust topological feature vectors can be seamlessly used within state-of-the-art architectures such as Swin Transformers. We establish theoretical guarantees for the stability of our vectorization under generalized Wasserstein metrics. Our experiments on benchmark medical imaging and computer vision datasets show the benefit CuMPerLay on classification and segmentation performance, particularly in limited-data scenarios. Overall, CuMPerLay offers a promising direction for integrating global structural information into deep networks for structured image analysis.

1 Introduction

In recent years, computer vision has witnessed remarkable advancements driven by deep learning (DL) techniques, leading to breakthroughs in classification, segmentation, and object detection. However, despite their success, DL models often struggle to effectively capture the intricate geometric and topological structures inherent in image data [12, 84, 50, 82]. These limitations have spurred interest in complementary approaches that can provide a more holistic understanding of image content by incorporating global structural information beyond pixel-wise feature extraction.

A promising direction is topological data analysis [13] (TDA), which provides a rigorous framework for analyzing high-order structures in data. Persistent homology (PH), in particular, has been widely applied to extract topological descriptors that capture shape and connectivity in complex datasets [30]. A more recent and advanced variant, multiparameter persistence [46] (MP), extends this approach by tracking multiple filtrations, allowing it to encode a finer-grained representation [9] and enabling the extraction of richer structural features [25]. While MP has shown considerable success in graph representation learning and point cloud analysis [28, 56], its application to image analysis remains relatively unexplored, arguably due to the vectorization algorithms suited for cubical complexes, the native topological structure of images.

In this work, we introduce CuMPerLay, a novel, differentiable vectorization layer for multiparameter persistence over cubical complexes. While incorporating topological features from single-parameter persistence (SP) is relatively standard [15, 6, 27], extending this to the cubical MP (CMP) setting is highly non-trivial. We propose to decompose the CMP into a differentiable combination of individual, learnable single filtrations. We then deploy CuMPerLay as a differentiable layer within a deep architecture, particularly Swin transformers [54]. Our theoretical analysis shows that CuMPerLay shows improved stability when compared to SP counterparts. By seamlessly integrating CMP into deep networks in an end-to-end manner, our layer helps discerning topological features essential for structured image analysis.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a differentiable, novel vectorization for Cubical Multiparameter Persistence, combining learnable filtration functions with learnable vectorizations, and integrate into state-of-the-art image-based learning pipelines.

  • •

    We theoretically prove the stability of our CuMPerLay along with a family of other filtration functions we devise.

  • •

    We propose a hybrid DL model integrating CMP with Swin transformers, demonstrating synergistic improvements.

  • •

    Finally, to the best of our knowledge, we develop the first (publicly available) CUDA GPU implementation of Cubical Persistence and Cubical Multiparameter Persistence.

Our experiments on benchmark medical imaging and computer vision datasets show that our topological vectors improve model performance in both standard and limited-data scenarios. Our sources can be found under: https://github.com/circle-group/cumperlay.

2 Related Work

TDA in image analysis

TDA has become a powerful tool in image processing, extracting high-level structural features invariant to transformations like rotation and noise. Early studies [4] applied TDA to brain MRI scans, distinguishing normal and pathological structures. More recent works [23, 80, 63] integrated PH with DL, improving feature extraction and interpretability. Similarly, [83, 81] showed TDA-based features enhance deep networks in histopathological image classification by capturing robust cellular representations. TDA has also improved image denoising [68], demonstrating PH preserves geometric structures while filtering noise.

Other studies used TDA as a topological loss function to enforce structural constraints during training. [43] introduced a topological signature layer for CNNs, enabling end-to-end learning of PH features, while [35] proposed a differentiable topological loss to optimize structure persistence, improving medical image segmentation. The incorporation of topological features has significantly enhanced CNNs [79, 23, 80, 67, 72, 48]. For a comprehensive review of TDA in biomedicine, see [70]. PHG-Net [63] incorporated cubical single-persistence topological features using a PointNet [64]-based encoder into recent architectures like Swin Transformers [54] and SENet [44]. Future research will refine topological priors, differentiable persistence computations [16], and domain-specific loss functions.

Multiparameter Persistence (MP). MP theory enhances single persistence by capturing topological features from multidimensional filtrations, but theoretical challenges—such as the partially ordered threshold set—have hindered its adoption in machine learning (See suppl. material for detailed discussion). Most methods rely on slicing to produce one-dimensional persistence diagrams [53, 14], leading to information loss and dependence on slicing directions [9]. Alternatives extend persistence landscapes to higher dimensions, improving representation at the cost of increased complexity [77]. Recently, Loiseaux et al. [56] introduced stable vectorization using signed barcodes as Radon measures, generating robust feature vectors. While effective for point clouds and graphs, these methods do not generalize to the cubical complexes considered here.

MP has shown promise in graph representation learning [57, 28] but remains underexplored in image analysis. Notable exceptions include [21], which applied MP to mathematical morphology for topology-aware image processing and denoising, achieving results comparable to deep learning. Expanding on this, [22] quantified mitochondrial branching morphology to study gene mutations affecting structure. While prior works focus on specific filtrations and Betti numbers, we extend MP analysis across diverse contexts and introduce flexible vectorization methods for MP modules, enabling integration into downstream DL tasks.

3 Background

We dedicate this section to exposing the less commonly known cubical complexes and cubical multipersistence to computer vision community with a bottom-up construction. Our exposition is inspired by [46, 30, 25].

3.1 Cubical Persistence

Definition 1 (Elementary interval).

An elementary interval or a 11-cube, is a closed interval I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R}: I=[l,l+1]I=[l,l+1] for some l∈ℤl\in\mathbb{Z}. We denote [l]=[l,l][l]=[l,l] for a point or 0-cube, and I=[0,1]I=[0,1] the unit interval.

Definition 2 (Elementary cube).

A dd-dimensional elementary cube or dd-cube QQ is the product of finitely many elementary intervals Q=I1×I2×⋯×Id∈ℝdQ=I_{1}\times I_{2}\times\cdots\times I_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Intuitively, the elementary cubes of a 3D grid include vertices, edges, squares (22-cubes) and voxels (33-cubes).

Definition 3 (Boundary).

A boundary of an elementary interval II is composed of its two endpoints: ∂I=∂[l,l+1]=[l+1,l+1]−[l,l]={l,l+1}\partial I=\partial[l,l+1]=[l+1,l+1]-[l,l]=\{l,l+1\}. The boundary of a cube is the set of its (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional faces, and is a chain obtained in the following way:

∂Q=⋃i=1d(I1×⋯∂Ii×⋯Id).\partial Q=\bigcup_{i=1}^{d}\left(I_{1}\times\cdots\partial I_{i}\times\cdots I_{d}\right). (1)
Definition 4 (Face).

For two elementary cubes QQ and Q′Q^{\prime}, we define QQ to be a face of Q′Q^{\prime}, denoted Q⊆Q′Q\subseteq Q^{\prime}, if Ii⊂Ii′I_{i}\subset I_{i}^{\prime} for all i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d. Similarly, PP is said to be a coface of QQ.

Definition 5 (Cubical complex (CC)).

An (elementary) cubical complex 𝒦\mathcal{K} is the union of a set of dd-cubes such that:

  1. 1.

    For every Q∈𝒦Q\in\mathcal{K}, if P⊆QP\subseteq Q, then P∈𝒦P\in\mathcal{K}.

  2. 2.

    If Q∈𝒦Q\in\mathcal{K}, then all faces of QQ are also in 𝒦\mathcal{K}.

Intuitively, a CC represents a grid as a cell complex with cells of all dimensions as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Definition 6 (Cubical map).

A map h:𝒦→𝒦′h:\mathcal{K}\to\mathcal{K}^{\prime} is said to be cubical if Q⊆Q′∈𝒦⟹h⁡(Q)⊆h⁡(Q′)∈𝒦′Q\subseteq Q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}\implies h(Q)\subseteq h(Q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{K}^{\prime}.

Definition 7 (Chain complex of a CC).

A nn-chain is a formal finite sum11 1 For a set SS and a free Abelian group on SS, the formal finite sum ff is an element of ⨁s∈Sℤ={f:S→ℤ|{s∈S∣f(s)≠0} is finite}\bigoplus_{s\in S}\mathbb{Z}=\left\{f:S\to\mathbb{Z}\;\middle|\;\{s\in S\mid f(s)\neq 0\}\text{ is finite}\right\}. of nn-dimensional cubes with integer coefficients. A chain group CnC_{n} is the (free Abelian) group generated by the set of nn-dimensional cubes in the complex. The cubical chain complex C⋆​(𝒦)C_{\star}(\mathcal{K}) of a CC is the sequence of chain groups and boundary operators given by:

⋯→∂n+1Cn​(𝒦)→∂nCn−1​(𝒦)→∂n−1⋯→∂1C0​(𝒦)→0.\displaystyle\cdots\xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}}C_{n}(\mathcal{K})\xrightarrow{\partial_{n}}C_{n-1}(\mathcal{K})\xrightarrow{\partial_{n-1}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\partial_{1}}C_{0}(\mathcal{K})\to 0.

The boundary operators satisfy ∂n∘∂n+1=0\partial_{n}\circ\partial_{n+1}=0 for all nn.

The topological structure of a CC is characterized by identifying its holes, defined as cycles that are not boundaries of other objects. This notion can be made rigorous as follows:

Definition 8 (Homology).

For a cubical chain complex, a nn-chain z∈Cnz\in C_{n} is called a cycle (closed loop) if ∂n(z)=0\partial_{n}(z)=0. Every boundary is a cycle, so Bn​(𝒦)⊆Zn​(𝒦)B_{n}(\mathcal{K})\subseteq Z_{n}(\mathcal{K}). The set of nn-cycles Zn​(𝒦)Z_{n}(\mathcal{K}) and the set of boundary elements Bn​(𝒦)B_{n}(\mathcal{K}) are then defined as:

Zn​(𝒦)\displaystyle Z_{n}(\mathcal{K}) :=ker(∂n)={c∈Cn(𝒦)∣∂n(c)=0}\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\ker(\partial_{n})=\{c\in C_{n}(\mathcal{K})\mid\partial_{n}(c)=0\} (2)
Bn​(𝒦)\displaystyle B_{n}(\mathcal{K}) :=im(∂n+1)={∂n+1(c)∣c∈Cn+1(𝒦)}\displaystyle\vcentcolon=\mathrm{im}(\partial_{n+1})=\{\partial_{n+1}(c)\mid c\in C_{n+1}(\mathcal{K})\} (3)

Taking the group of cycles Zn​(𝒦)Z_{n}(\mathcal{K}) and factoring out the cycles which act as boundaries Bn​(𝒦)B_{n}(\mathcal{K}) to higher dimensional cubes in the complex, we are left with the nthn^{\mathrm{th}} cubical homology group, Hn​(𝒦)H_{n}(\mathcal{K}), capturing all the nn-dimensional holes:

Hn(𝒦)=Zn(𝒦)/Bn(𝒦)=ker(∂n)/im(∂n+1).\displaystyle H_{n}(\mathcal{K})={Z_{n}(\mathcal{K})}/{B_{n}(\mathcal{K})}={\ker(\partial_{n})}/{\mathrm{im}(\partial_{n+1})}. (4)

The homology of XX is the collection of all homology groups: H⋆​(𝒦)={Hn​(𝒦)}n∈ℤH_{\star}(\mathcal{K})=\left\{H_{n}(\mathcal{K})\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}.

To extend the notion of homology to persistent homology, we need the concept of a filtration:

Definition 9 (Filtration).

A filtration is a finite (or countable) sequence of nested cubical complexes (subcomplexes):

∅=𝒦0⊆𝒦1⊆⋯⊆𝒦n−1⊆𝒦n=𝒦.\displaystyle\emptyset=\mathcal{K}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{n-1}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{n}=\mathcal{K}. (5)

A filtration function f𝒦:𝒦→ℝf_{\mathcal{K}}:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R} describes the filtration by assigning to each dd-cube the first index at which it appears in the complex, capturing the notion that a cube cannot appear strictly before its faces: f𝒦​(P)≤f𝒦​(Q),∀P⊂Qf_{\mathcal{K}}(P)\leq f_{\mathcal{K}}(Q),\,\forall P\subset Q. The sublevel set 𝒦i:=𝒦⁡(ai)\mathcal{K}_{i}:=\mathcal{K}(a_{i}) corresponding to ai∈ℝa_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is defined by f𝒦−1(−∞,ai]f_{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}(-\infty,a_{i}], a subcomplex of 𝒦\mathcal{K}.

Example 1 (Threshold filtrations).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a 2D grayscale image with pixels {Δi​j⊂𝒳}\{\Delta_{ij}\subset\mathcal{X}\} and intensity values Ii​j∈[0,255]I_{ij}\in[0,255] for an M×NM\times N grid. Given a sequence of thresholds 0=τ1<τ2<⋯<τT=2550=\tau_{1}<\tau_{2}<\cdots<\tau_{T}=255, we obtain a nested sequence of binary images 𝒳1⊂𝒳2⊂⋯⊂𝒳T\mathcal{X}_{1}\subset\mathcal{X}_{2}\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal{X}_{T}, where 𝒳T={Δi​j⊂𝒳∣Ii​j≤τT}\mathcal{X}_{T}=\{\Delta_{ij}\subset\mathcal{X}\mid I_{ij}\leq\tau_{T}\} (see Fig. 2). This process, known as sublevel filtration, starts with a blank image and activates pixels as their grayscale values reach the threshold τT\tau_{T}. Conversely, activating pixels in descending order yields a superlevel filtration. For a color image, one can use individual color channels, e.g., (Ri​j,Gi​j,Bi​j)(R_{ij},G_{ij},B_{ij}), for filtration. More generally, any nested sequence 𝒳t⊂𝒳t+1\mathcal{X}_{t}\subset\mathcal{X}_{t+1} defines a filtration, independent of grayscale values or other functions.

In suppl. material, we present key bifiltration methods that have the potential to significantly enhance the performance of single-parameter homology in several settings.

We are now ready to state the definitions that will lead to the construction of cubical persistent homology.

Definition 10.

Any cubical map 𝒦i→𝒦j\mathcal{K}_{i}\to\mathcal{K}_{j} induces a linear map between the homology spaces due to functoriality: ιi​j:Hk​(𝒦i)→Hk​(𝒦j)\iota_{ij}:H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{i})\to H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{j}) for i≤ji\leq j. Applying this on the filtration in Eq 5 leads to a sequence of homology groups:

Hk(𝒦0)→ι01Hk(𝒦1)→ι12⋯Hk(𝒦n−1)→ιn−1,nHk(𝒦n).\displaystyle H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{0})\xrightarrow{\iota_{01}}H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{1})\xrightarrow{\iota_{12}}\cdots H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{n-1})\xrightarrow{\iota_{n-1,n}}H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{n}).
Definition 11 (Cubical Persistent Homology (CPH)).

The sequence in Dfn. 10 is known to be the persistence module:

𝒫={Hk​(𝒦i),ιi​j}0≤i≤j≤n,\mathcal{P}=\left\{H_{k}\left(\mathcal{K}_{i}\right),\iota_{ij}\right\}_{0\leq i\leq j\leq n}, (6)

and defines the kthk^{\mathrm{th}} CPH, essentially keeping track of how kk-holes (kk-dimensional voids) appear and disappear as we move from 𝒦0\mathcal{K}_{0} to 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n}. CBH records these homological changes through birth times b⁡(σ)b(\sigma) and death times d⁡(σ)d(\sigma):

bσ:=b⁡(σ)\displaystyle b_{\sigma}:=b(\sigma) :=inf{j∈I∣σ∈Im​ιj​i}\displaystyle:=\inf\left\{j\in I\mid\sigma\in\mathrm{Im}\iota_{ji}\right\} (7)
dσ:=d⁡(σ)\displaystyle d_{\sigma}:=d(\sigma) :=inf{j∈I∣σ∉Im​ιj​i}.\displaystyle:=\inf\left\{j\in I\mid\sigma\notin\mathrm{Im}\iota_{ji}\right\}. (8)

The persistence of a kk-hole σ\sigma refers to its lifespan, dσ−bσd_{\sigma}-b_{\sigma} and the collection of half-open intervals (bars) {[bσ,dσ)}\{[b_{\sigma},d_{\sigma})\} is called a persistence barcode.

Definition 12 (Persistence Diagram (PD)).

The kthk^{\mathrm{th}} persistence diagram PDk\mathrm{PD}_{k} comprises all birth and death pairs of kk-holes in the filtration 𝒦^={𝒦i}i=0n\widehat{\mathcal{K}}=\{\mathcal{K}_{i}\}_{i=0}^{n}:

PDk​(𝒦^)={(bσ,dσ)∣σ∈Hk​(𝒦i)​ for ​bσ≤i<dσ}.\mathrm{PD}_{k}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}})=\{(b_{\sigma},d_{\sigma})\mid\sigma\in H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{i})\mbox{ for }b_{\sigma}\leq i<d_{\sigma}\}.

Persistence Diagrams (PDs), consisting of collections of 22-tuples, are not practical for utilization with ML tools. Instead, a common strategy is to transform PDs into a vector, a process referred to as vectorization [2].

Definition 13 (Vectorization).

A vectorization of a PD is a map Ψ:PD→ℝM\Psi:\mathrm{PD}\to\mathbb{R}^{M} from the space of PDs to a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space, linearly representing the PD and allowing standard vector-based methods to be applied.

Remark 1 (On computation).

In practice, PDs can be efficiently computed via linear algebra as done in various efficient and robust C++ / Python libraries such as Ripser [76], Gudhi [8], and Giotto [75]. Effective vectorizations can also be obtained by embeddings [1], kernels [49], or neural networks as done in Perslay [15]. MP for simplicial complexes can be computed through multipers\mathrm{multipers} (CPU-only). We release the first GPU implementation of MP involving CCs and share the pseudocode for our algorithm in suppl. material.

We call PH applied on a single-parameter filtration, single persistence (SP), and next present multipersistence (MP).

3.2 Cubical Multiparameter Persistence

We now extend the definitions in the previous sections to the multiparameter setting, constructed via a multifiltration:

Definition 14 (Multifiltration).

Given a CC 𝒦\mathcal{K}, let I1,I2,…,ImI_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{m} be totally ordered index sets, e.g. Ii={0,1,…,Ni}I_{i}=\{0,1,\ldots,N_{i}\}, or intervals in ℝ\mathbb{R}. A multifiltration of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is a family of subcomplexes

{𝒦t1,t2,…,tm⊆𝒦}(t1,t2,…,tm)∈I1×I2×⋯×Im\Bigl\{\mathcal{K}_{t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{m}}\subseteq\mathcal{K}\,\Bigr\}_{(t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{m})\in I_{1}\times I_{2}\times\cdots\times I_{m}} (9)

satisfying the monotonicity condition: if (t1,t2,…,tm)≤(s1,s2,…,sm)(t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{m})\leq(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{m}), i.e., ti≤si​ for all ​i=1,…,mt_{i}\leq s_{i}\text{ for all }i=1,\dots,m, then 𝒦t1,t2,…,tm⊆𝒦s1,s2,…,sm\mathcal{K}_{t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{m}}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{m}}: the subcomplexes are nested simultaneously with respect to each parameter. If m=2m=2, this is known to be a bifiltration. Similar to Dfn. 9, we speak of a bifiltration function F𝒦:𝒦→ℝ2F_{\mathcal{K}}:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}^{2} generating the sequence 𝒦t1,t2=F𝒦−1​(Δt1,t2)\mathcal{K}_{t_{1},t_{2}}=F_{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}(\Delta_{t_{1},t_{2}}) in Eq 9 where Δt1,t2=(−∞,t1]×(∞,t2]⊂ℝ2\Delta_{t_{1},t_{2}}=(-\infty,t_{1}]\times(\infty,t_{2}]\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}.

In what follows, we explicitly focus on bifiltrations of 2D images. Though, our construction extends naturally to higher dimensions, for example 3D voxel grids. For 2D images, there are numerous ways to construct bifiltrations, such as employing morphological operations [21] or thresholding [25]. We give details of these bifiltrations in our suppl. material. It is important to note that determining an optimal bifiltration is a complex challenge and remains an active area of research. In this work, as we discuss in Sec. 4.1, we opt for learning bifiltrations in a data-driven manner.

We now state the biparameter persistence for CCs in a vein similar to SP:

Definition 15 (Cubical biparameter persistence).

Similar to Dfn. 11, but this time for any index pairs (s,t),(s′,t′)(s,t),(s^{\prime},t^{\prime}) with (s,t)≤(s′,t′)(s,t)\leq(s^{\prime},t^{\prime}) that is s≤s′s\leq s^{\prime} and t≤t′t\leq t^{\prime}, the inclusion map 𝒦(s,t)↪𝒦(s′,t′)\mathcal{K}_{(}s,t)\hookrightarrow\mathcal{K}_{(}s^{\prime},t^{\prime}) induces a homomorphism on homology:

ι(s,t),(s′,t′):Hk​(𝒦s,t)→Hk​(𝒦s′,t′),\iota_{({s,t}),({s^{\prime},t^{\prime}})}:H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{s,t})\to H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}), (10)

and the collection

𝒫k′​(𝒦)={Hk​(𝒦s,t),ι(s,t),(s′,t′)}(s,t),\mathcal{P}_{k}^{\prime}(\mathcal{K})=\left\{H_{k}\left(\mathcal{K}_{s,t}\right),\iota_{(s,t),(s^{\prime},t^{\prime})}\right\}_{(s,t)}, (11)

defines the cubical biparameter persistent kk-homology.

Remark 2 (On multiparameter vectorizations).

Unlike SP, there is no natural and precise extension of PD (or its vectorization) to MP outputs, primarily due to the partial ordering problem (See suppl. material). In a single filtration, the sequence {𝒦n}\{\mathcal{K}_{n}\} is fully ordered and the region where a topological feature σ\sigma persists would form a clear 1D interval ℐσ\mathcal{I}_{\sigma}, easily expressed by (bσ,dσ)(b_{\sigma},d_{\sigma}). In multifiltrations, this becomes highly complicated as the shape of the region ℐσ\mathcal{I}_{\sigma} might not resemble a perfect rectangle [9, 57]. Moreover, ordering a multifiltration {𝒦s,t}\{\mathcal{K}_{s,t}\} for every pair of indices is far from trivial, e.g., 𝒦2,5\mathcal{K}_{2,5} is not comparable to 𝒦3,4\mathcal{K}_{3,4}. Even with assumptions like barcode decomposability, expressing ℐσ\mathcal{I}_{\sigma} with birth and death indices becomes unfeasible unless ℐσ\mathcal{I}_{\sigma} is a perfect rectangle.

On the other hand, there are readily available invariants for a multipersistence module. For example, for any pair (s,t)(s,t) and (s′,t′)(s^{\prime},t^{\prime}) the rank of the map ι(s,t),(s′,t′):Hk​(𝒦s,t)→Hk​(𝒦s′,t′)\iota_{({s,t}),({s^{\prime},t^{\prime}})}:H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{s,t})\to H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}) is well-defined, and called rank invariant of the bipersistence module [9]. Similarly, ℋ:I1×…​I2→ℤ\mathcal{H}:I_{1}\times\dots I_{2}\to\mathbb{Z} with ℋ⁡(s,t)=rank​Hk​(𝒦s,t)\mathcal{H}(s,t)=\mbox{rank}H_{k}(\mathcal{K}_{s,t}) is called Hilbert function of the bipersistence module. Our proposed CuMPerLay, which we will introduce next, is a general MP vectorization for CCs, designed to address the aforementioned problem.

4 CuMPer: Cubical MultiPersistence

4.1 Differentiable CuMPerLay Vectorization

We circumvent the aforementioned obstacles by employing a technique known as slicing, involving the formation of horizontal slices on a MP grid of M×NM\times N, where we generate a series of single-parameter filtrations denoted as {𝒦s,⋅}1M\{\mathcal{K}_{s,\cdot}\}_{1}^{M}. Next, by applying SP vectorizations to these individual filtrations, we derive MM distinct vectors. More formally:

Proposition 1 (CuMPerLay).

We introduce our cubical two-parameter vectorization ΨMP\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}} to be:

ΨMP​(𝒦)=ρ⁡([[Ψ⁡(PD0​(𝒦s,⋅))Ψ⁡(PD1​(𝒦s,⋅))]]t),\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}\left(\mathcal{K}\right)=\rho\left(\left[\begin{bmatrix}\Psi\left(\mathrm{PD}_{0}\left(\mathcal{K}_{s,\cdot}\right)\right)\\ \Psi\left(\mathrm{PD}_{1}\left(\mathcal{K}_{s,\cdot}\right)\right)\end{bmatrix}\right]_{t}\right), (12)

where we choose the SP vectorization Ψ\Psi for the sths^{\mathrm{th}} row of the filtration to be a level-dependent PersLay [15]:

Ψ⁡(PD⁡(𝒦⋅,t)):=op⁡({wt​(p)⋅ϕt​(p)}p∈PD⁡(𝒦s,⋅)).\Psi(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{K}_{\cdot,t})):=\mathrm{op}\left(\{w_{t}(p)\cdot\phi_{t}(p)\}_{p\in\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{K}_{s,\cdot})}\right). (13)

While a family of choices are possible for the functions op\mathrm{op}, wtw_{t} and ϕt\phi_{t}, in this work, we make the specific choices. op\mathrm{op} denotes the sum\mathrm{sum}. Given weights 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t}, wt​(b,d∣𝐰t):=|d−b|𝐰tw_{t}(b,d\,\mid\,\mathbf{w}_{t}):=|d-b|^{\mathbf{w}_{t}} denotes the power weighting function for each persistence pair. The transformation function follows the triangle point transformation ϕt=ϕΛ:ℝ2→ℝq\phi_{t}=\phi_{\Lambda}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{q} sends p↦[Λp​(t1),Λp​(t2),…,Λp​(tq)]⊤p\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_{p}(t_{1}),\Lambda_{p}(t_{2}),\dots,\Lambda_{p}(t_{q})\end{bmatrix}^{\top}, where q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and

Λp:t↦max⁡{0,0.5​(d−b)−|t−0.5​(b+d)|}.\Lambda_{p}\colon t\mapsto\max\{0,0.5(d-b)-|t-0.5(b+d)|\}. (14)

Finally, the aggregator ρ:PD2×Nt→ℝD\rho:\mathrm{PD}^{2\times N_{t}}\to\mathbb{R}^{D} summarizes the information into a single vector.

Remark 3 (On differentiability and learnability).

Eq 12 forms a Silhouette representation [18] that can be learned separately for each row in the MP. In particular, the weights 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t} as well as the transformation times t1,…,tq∈ℝt_{1},\dots,t_{q}\in\mathbb{R} remain learnable, as well as the parameters of the aggregation function ρ\rho, which we model as a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). We implement the Cubical PH in CUDA and propagate straight-through gradients to pixel locations that produce the corresponding persistence pairs, followed by a differentiable row-wise vectorization. This allows us to learn the parameters of the inverse filtration functions f𝒦−1f_{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}, which we model as neural nets (Sec. 4.2) to produce {𝒦s,t}\{\mathcal{K}_{s,t}\}.

Stability theorem.  Given the technical challenges of obtaining multipersistence outputs like persistence diagrams, we circumvent this by using slicing, a standard method in the field. By applying horizontal slices to an M×NM\times N multipersistence grid, we generate single persistence (SP) filtrations {𝒳^i}1M\{\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i}\}_{1}^{M}. Using SP vectorizations, we obtain MM vectors φ→i=φ⁡(PD⁡(𝒳^i))\vec{\varphi}_{i}=\varphi(\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i})), which are then arranged as rows in a 2D tensor ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}, termed the induced MP vectorization of φ\varphi.

Here, we prove that if the original SP vectorization φ\varphi is stable (see suppl. material), then so is its induced MP vectorization ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi} with respect to the generalized metrics. These metrics represent natural extensions of the Wasserstein metric to multipersistence modules (see suppl. material).

Theorem 1 (Stability of induced MP vectorization).

Let φ\varphi be a stable SP vectorization22 2 All SP vectorizations considered in this work are stable. We make this notion precise in our suppl. material. φ\varphi need not necessarily correspond to the one in Eq 12.. Let ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi} denote the induced MP vectorization obtained by collecting mm separate vectors φt=φ⁡(PD⁡(𝒦s,⋅))\varphi_{t}=\varphi(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{K}_{s,\cdot})) into a 22-tensor, ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}. Then, there exists a constant C^φ>0\widehat{C}_{\varphi}>0 s.t. for any pair of CCs 𝒦1\mathcal{K}^{1} and 𝒦2\mathcal{K}^{2}:

𝔇⁡(ℳφ​(𝒦1),ℳφ​(𝒦2))≤Cφ⋅∑i=1m𝒲p​(PD⁡(𝒦^i1),PD⁡(𝒦^i−​2)CLOSE,\resizebox{32561971}{}{$\mathfrak{D}(\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}(\mathcal{K}^{1}),\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}(\mathcal{K}^{2}))\leq C_{\varphi}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{W}_{p}(\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{i}^{1}),\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{i}^{-}2)$},

where 𝒲p\mathcal{W}_{p} denotes the pp-Wasserstein distance on PDs and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} specifies a distance on the induced vectorizations

𝔇⁡(ℳφ​(𝒦1),ℳφ​(𝒦2))=∑i=1md⁡(φ⁡(𝒦i1),φ⁡(𝒦i2)),\mathfrak{D}(\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}(\mathcal{K}^{1}),\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}(\mathcal{K}^{2}))=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}(\varphi(\mathcal{K}^{1}_{i}),\varphi(\mathcal{K}^{2}_{i})), (15)

where d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is a metric, usually chosen to be the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance.

As Perslay vectorizations are stable, we can use Thm. 1 to prove the stability of CuMPerLay:

Corollary 1 (CuMPerLay is stable).

Let ΨMP\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}} represent CuMPerLay vectorization defined in Sec. 4.1. Let F,G:𝒦→ℝ2F,G:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}^{2} be bifiltration functions on 𝒦\mathcal{K} and 𝒦^F,𝒦^G\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F},\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{G} be the induced bipersistence modules. Then, we have

𝔇⁡(ΨMP​(𝒦^F),ΨMP​(𝒦^G))≤C^ΨMP​‖F−G‖∞\mathfrak{D}(\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}),\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{G}))\leq\widehat{C}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}}\|F-G\|_{\infty} (16)

Our suppl. material provides the required proofs.

4.2 Topology Aware Learning via CuMPerLay

To learn multifiltration functions end-to-end, we designed a Learnable Cubical MultiPersistence layer that can be integrated with existing deep learning networks, like common CNNs [42, 73, 44, 55] and Vision Transformers [32, 54]. Our module consists of four main parts: (i) a multifiltration decoder, (ii) a differentiable GPU Cubical Multipersistence block, (iii) the differentiable CuMPerLay vectorization module, and (iv) a fusion block.

Multifiltration decoder.   The multifiltration decoder takes the input image or activations from any network layer and upsamples it using a convolutional network into the image resolution desired for persistent homology calculations. It then outputs a multifiltration in 2 dimensions using a thresholding block for enforcing the filtration structure for each row of the multifiltration and a regularization loss for enforcing the filtration structure for each column. The input to the multifiltration decoder consists of multi-channel 𝐗∈ℝC′×H′×W′\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{C^{\prime}\times H^{\prime}\times W^{\prime}} features, corresponding to the activations obtained from the neural network or the input image. For a MP grid of M×NM\times N, the decoder outputs a MM-channel image 𝐙=[𝐙1,𝐙2,…,𝐙M]T∈[0,1]M×Hs×Ws\mathbf{Z}=[\mathbf{Z}_{1},\mathbf{Z}_{2},\dotsc,\mathbf{Z}_{M}]^{T}\in[0,1]^{M\times H_{s}\times W_{s}} with Hs,WsH_{s},W_{s} image size desired for persistent homology process, with sigmoid activation at last layer and min-max normalization over all rows. Then, for the sths^{\mathrm{th}} row, a NN-step staircase function with straight through gradients [5] is used for enforcing the multifiltration structure:

𝐙s′=⌊N​𝐙s⌋∈{0,1,…,N}Hs×Ws\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s}=\lfloor N\mathbf{Z}_{s}\rfloor\in\{0,1,\dotsc,N\}^{H_{s}\times W_{s}} (17)

This function maps the continuous multifiltration decoder outputs to N+1 values corresponding to N values in each row in the MP grid, creating a single persistence structure per row. This process can also be viewed as a learnable alternative to sublevel filtration. We call 𝐙s′\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s} the compact multifiltration representation. The multifiltration {𝒦s,t}\{\mathcal{K}_{s,t}\} can be obtained from this representation via {𝒦s,t}=1\{\mathcal{K}_{s,t}\}=1 if 𝐙s′=t−1\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s}=t-1, 00 otherwise for 1≤t≤N1\leq t\leq N at each pixel location. We utilize a convolutional network with upsampling layers for the multifiltration decoder, as checkboard artifacts that can be seen in the deconvolution layers [60] can result in checkboard pattern artifacts in the multifiltration output, resulting in undesired persistence pairs.

Persistence and vectorization.   The compact multifiltration outputs are then utilized to obtain persistence pairs corresponding to each row in the multifiltration. Throughout this process, the gradients are backpropagated into pixels in the multifiltration that produce the corresponding birth and death values. Then, our differentiable CuMPerLay vectorization module produces learnable vectorizations using these persistence pairs. We use the power weighting function with learnable powers 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t} and the triangle point transformation with learnable times t1,…,tq∈ℝt_{1},\dots,t_{q}\in\mathbb{R} in vectorization. We obtain the vectorizations as HH-dimensional latent features 𝐯s∈ℝH\mathbf{v}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{H} for each row ss in the multifiltration with the summation aggregation. These vectorizations are then concatenated into a single vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} corresponding to our MP vectorization in Fig. 3.

Fusion block.   The fusion block recalibrates channel-wise activations from the original network with a residual gated linear unit [26] with bias:

FB⁡(𝐗,𝐯)=𝐗+𝐗⊗σ⁡(𝐖1​𝐯)+𝐖2​𝐯,\mathrm{FB}\left(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{v}\right)=\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{X}\otimes\sigma\left(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{v}\right)+\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathbf{v},\vskip-5.69054pt (18)

where 𝐗\mathbf{X} is the original activations, 𝐯\mathbf{v} is the MP vectorization, 𝐖i\mathbf{W}_{i} are the learnable weights, and σ\sigma is the sigmoid function. We further concatenate the additional vectorization coming from a Learnable Cubical MultiPersistence layer on the input image to the vectorization 𝐯\mathbf{v} obtained in each layer.

Multifiltration regularization.  We utilize a soft regularization loss to enforce the single filtration structure in each column. While the initial continuous output from the multifiltration decoder does not respect the bifiltration structure described before, Eq 17 enforces this bifiltration-ness on each row, similar to a sublevel set filtration. The compact representations 𝐙s′\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s} follow a structure induced by the bifiltration {𝒦s,⋅}\{\mathcal{K}_{s,\cdot}\}, (𝐙s′≥𝐙s+1′\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s}\geq\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s+1} for 1≤s≤M−11\leq s\leq M-1). Our regularization loss is then formulated as:

ℒreg=∑s=1M−1max⁡(0,𝐙s+1′−𝐙s′)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\sum_{s=1}^{M-1}\max(0,\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s+1}-\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}_{s}) (19)

This regularization guides the output of our multifiltration decoders to produce a single filtration structure on the columns. Together with the original row-wise single filtration, this ensures a multifiltration structure on our 2-parameter learned filtration. Following PHG-Net [63], we add a topological classification head as a two-layer MLP with a cross-entropy (CE) loss ℒTopo\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Topo}} to guide the multifiltration decoders and vectorization layers, in addition to the normal cross-entropy loss ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}. We use a negative local image entropy [37] loss on the compact filtration outputs ℒLE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LE}} to increase locality, promote early exploration of multifiltrations, and facilitate the training of the learnable cubical MP blocks. The multifiltration decoder models the inverse filtration functions f𝒦−1f_{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}, and can be learned together with the vectorization module and the fusion block by utilizing the differentiability of the persistent homology and the vectorization steps. The layer can be repeated and used after any block in the original network (e.g. after each Swin Transformer Block in Swin V2 [54]), and gradients can be backpropagated to the network. We give sample learned bifiltration examples in Fig. 5 and further examples in the suppl. material.

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

Datasets.  We use three publicly available medical imaging datasets and one computer vision dataset. The first dataset ISIC 2018 dataset consists of dermoscopic images of skin lesions, curated to facilitate automated melanoma classification [24]. The dataset comprises 10,015 images spanning seven diagnostic categories. This dataset is part of the ISIC Challenge series and serves as a benchmark for skin lesion classification models. We use the official split for train, validation, and test subsets. The second dataset CBIS-DDSM is a large-scale mammogram dataset for breast cancer diagnosis [51]. It contains 3568 mammogram images, with 2111 benign and 1457 malignant cases. We utilize the official train and test split with a further 80:20 train/validation split. The third dataset Glaucoma is from publicly available Eye Disease Image Dataset (Eye-DID), a comprehensive collection of color fundus images for retinal disease classification [69, 65]. Specifically, we utilized 1024 healthy and 1349 glaucoma fundus images for binary classification. The original 2004 × 1690 images were resized to 224×224 for computational efficiency. We used an 80:20 training/test split in this dataset, with an 80:20 split on the training portion for the validation set. Our fourth dataset PASCAL VOC 2012 [34] is a benchmark dataset for segmentation. We use the Semantic Boundaries [41] (SB) augmented version of the VOC dataset (excluding any VOC validation images). We use a 90:10 split on the training portion (7087 images) for the validation set. We utilize the VOC validation split as our test set (1449 images) and resize all images to 224×224.

Topological baselines.  To compare the standalone performance of topological models, we extract topological vectors with standard filtration functions (see suppl. material) through Multipersistence (MP) and Single Persistence (SP).

SP vectors: We compute Betti curves for each homology group using 100 bins, resulting in 100-dimensional vectors per homology group. The concatenation of features from both homology groups is directly used for classification.

MP vectors: For color images, we apply 10 thresholds per channel (Red, Green, and Blue), obtaining a persistence representation of shape (10 ×\times 10 ×\times 10) for each homology group, with two homology groups. For grayscale images, we apply 50 thresholds for grayscale and 10 erosion filtration levels [0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20], producing an array of shape (10, 50) per homology group. These features are flattened, and the top 300 features are selected using an XGBoost [19]-based feature importance ranking.

MLP Classifier: The extracted features from both MP and SP models are used as input to a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for classification. The network consists of two hidden layers with ReLU activation and 0.3 dropout. The model is trained using the Adam optimizer with cross-entropy loss.

Implementation details of our TopoSwin.

We use the SwinV2-B [54] variant as our base model and utilize one learnable cubical multipersistence module after each Swin transformer block, with an additional module on the input images. We use 8x16 MP grids in the multifiltration decoders, with 112x112 image size for the filtration image sizes, except for the module on input images that uses 224x224. We used 100 learnable sample locations for the triangle transformation function in our vectorization module. The base model in the Swin and TopoSwin variants is always initialized with pre-trained weights trained on the ImageNet-1K [29] dataset. We do not back-propagate gradients from multifiltration decoders back into the base network when utilizing pre-trained weights. We denote the single persistence variant of our model as TopoSwin-SP (TS-SP) and the multipersistence variant of our model as TopoSwin-MP (TS-MP).

We utilize AdamW [59] optimizer with a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} and weight decay of 0.01 for training our models. We do not use learning rate scheduling, use only random flip augmentations, and train for 100 epochs based on our hyperparameter tuning on the Swin baseline. We use 1.0 as ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} weight, 0.25 as ℒtopo\mathcal{L}_{\text{topo}} weight, and 0.01 as the ℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} weight, and 10−410^{-4} as the ℒLE\mathcal{L}_{\text{LE}} weight.

For our CUDA cubical multipersistence implementation, we implement a union-find based cubical persistence algorithm [78] to efficiently find 0th dimensional homology. We utilize the duality results between top-dimensional cell and vertex constructions of persistent homology [7] to calculate the 1st dimensional homology of 2D images by utilizing the same union-find algorithm on the dual construction. Our implementation is influenced by the CPU implementation of cubical single persistence CubicalRipser [47].

5.2 Results

Medical datasets

Tab. 1 presents our experimental results on the three independent medical datasets. The first two rows showcase the standalone performance of SP and MP vectors using traditional filtrations. Notably, MP consistently outperforms SP, highlighting that MP generates more informative feature vectors for image classification tasks, as expected. The third row reports the baseline deep learning (DL) model Swin Transformer V2 [54]. In the fourth row, we report PHG-Net [63], a hybrid topological model that integrates standard SP vectors with Swin V2. To ensure consistency, we evaluate these models using official/our data splits, with PHG-Net setup following their public code.

Finally, we introduce TopoSwin-Betti, our model incorporating MP Betti vectors with traditional filtrations. Our results indicate that the proposed hybrid models consistently enhance the performance of the Swin baseline while outperforming PHG-Net. The key distinctions between PHG-Net and our approach lie in feature extraction and learnable filtrations. While PHG-Net employs PointNet to process persistence diagrams derived from SP filtrations, our models utilize PersLay-based vectorizations with learnable filtrations.

We observe that TopoSwin-MP obtains best accuracy on Glaucoma with second-to-best accuracy on DDSM, with slightly better results from TopoSwin-SP. In addition, it obtains the best AUC on DDSM and ISIC with slightly lower AUC than TopoSwin-SP on Glaucoma. The results indicate consistent performance improvements of TopoSwin over baseline Swin model, with MP outperforming SP in many cases. In addition, we observe that TopoSwin-Betti outperforms Swin in ISIC and Glaucoma, while it underperforms in DDSM. This indicates while the standard MP features are helpful in DL scenarios, the end-to-end learnable MP features consistently provide better improvements.

Computer vision dataset

Tab. 2 presents our segmentation results on the VOC 2012 dataset.

We consider: (i) a Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) [58] with a ResNet-50 [42] backbone pretrained on ImageNet, and (ii) a U-Net [58] trained from scratch. For Topo-SP/MP variants, we follow the same persistence setup from TopoSwin for the FCN with the ResNet-backbone, and for U-net, the same persistence modules are placed over the skip connections. In both settings, while Topo-SP outperforms the baseline, our cubical MP variant delivers consistent and larger improvements in both mIoU and Acc.

Performance on limited data

We hypothesize that the robustness of topological vectors can serve as effective anchors, enhancing deep learning (DL) models’ ability to learn in data-scarce settings. Our experiments in limited data scenarios support this intuition, as shown in Fig. 6 and suppl. material. We used the same test sets across all datasets, systematically reducing the training data to 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, and 100% of the original training data. While performance variations exist across datasets, our hybrid models exhibit more stable trends as training data decreases. Overall, topological vectors do not degrade performance; instead, they contribute to more robust learning and yield performance improvements in several data-limited settings.

Ablation study.  In our ablation study, we assessed performance improvements by comparing TopoSwin-SP and TopoSwin-MP variants without CuMPerLay vectorization and image entropy loss, as well as the TopoSwin-Betti variant (Table 3). In the table, SPL denotes SP PersLay vectorization, and NEnp indicates no image entropy loss. Our vectorization outperforms SP PersLay, while removing image entropy loss hinders performance, suggesting reduced filtration learning. These results confirm that both image entropy and our vectorization enhance Swin model performance, with learnable vectorization surpassing standard filtrations.

We also compare our PersLay-based MP vectorization with single and multi-parameter persistent landscapes [11]. Our PersLay-based MP vectorization subsumes many popular vectorization methods such as persistence images, silhouettes, landscapes, and kernels, and outperforms persistence landscapes (Land.) in both DDSM and ISIC in terms of AUC, tabulated on the right (Tab. 4).

Runtime

Tab. 5 provides execution times (sec.) for 16×3216\times 32 cubical MPH on 224×224224\times 224 images, over 300 iterations with a batch size of 8. Our GPU version (on RTX 4090) is significantly faster than Gudhi [8] implementation and its parallelization over 24 processes (on Intel i9-12900K).

6 Conclusion

We introduced CuMPerLay, a novel differentiable vectorization layer for Cubical Multiparameter Persistence (CMP), effectively bridging TDA and DL, thanks to the end-to-end learnable multiparameter filtrations. By leveraging learnable MP with stable MP vectorization, we capture richer structural representations than SP and standard MP, improving feature extraction and enhancing downstream performance in SOTA DL models, particularly Swin Transformers.

Limitations & future work

While our approach demonstrates significant promise, further research is warranted to learn optimal bifiltrations and extend the framework to higher-dimensions and more diverse datasets. We are hopeful that our work will be helpful in improving topological machine learning tool-set [38, 62, 40, 39].

Appendix A Stability Results

A.1 Stability of Single Persistence Vectorizations

In machine learning, ensuring the stability of a particular persistence diagram (PD) vectorization is very crucial, as stability examines whether small changes in the PD result in significant alterations in the vectorization. To address this question, we need clear definitions of what constitutes ”small” and ”large” changes, which in turn requires a way to measure distance within the space of persistence diagrams. The most widely used metric for this purpose is the Wasserstein distance, also known as the matching distance.

Consider two images, 𝒳+\mathcal{X}^{+} and 𝒳−\mathcal{X}^{-}, with their associated persistence diagrams PD⁡(𝒳+)\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+}) and PD⁡(𝒳−)\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{-}), respectively (omitting dimension labels). Each diagram contains points {qj+}∪Δ+\{q_{j}^{+}\}\cup\Delta^{+} and {ql−}∪Δ−\{q_{l}^{-}\}\cup\Delta^{-}, where Δ±\Delta^{\pm} represents the diagonal (which stands for trivial cycles) with infinite multiplicity. Here, qj+=(bj+,dj+)q_{j}^{+}=(b_{j}^{+},d_{j}^{+}) in PD⁡(𝒳+)\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+}) denotes the birth and death times of a feature σj\sigma_{j} in 𝒳+\mathcal{X}^{+}. Let ϕ:PD⁡(𝒳+)→PD⁡(𝒳−)\phi:\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+})\to\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{-}) be a bijection, allowing mappings even when the cardinalities |{qj+}||\{q_{j}^{+}\}| and |{ql−}||\{q_{l}^{-}\}| differ. The pp-th Wasserstein distance, denoted 𝒲p\mathcal{W}_{p}, is formally defined as follows:

𝒲p​(PD⁡(𝒳+),PD⁡(𝒳−))=minϕ⁡(∑j‖qj+−ϕ⁡(qj+)‖∞p)1p,p∈ℤ+\mathcal{W}_{p}(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+}),\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{-}))=\min_{\phi}\biggl(\sum_{j}\|q_{j}^{+}-\phi(q_{j}^{+})\|_{\infty}^{p}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{p}},\quad p\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}.

 (20)

Next, a vectorization, denoted as φ⁡(PD⁡(𝒳))\varphi(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X})), is called to be stable if the distance between its outputs for two images, satisfies the inequality

d⁡(φ⁡(PD⁡(𝒳+)),φ⁡(PD⁡(𝒳−)))≤C⋅𝒲p​(PD⁡(𝒳+),PD⁡(𝒳−))\mathrm{d}(\varphi(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+})),\varphi(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{-})))\leq C\cdot\mathcal{W}_{p}(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+}),\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{-}))

where d(.,.)\mathrm{d}(.\ ,\ .) represents a suitable metric on the space of vectorizations. The constant C>0C>0 is independent of the images 𝒳±\mathcal{X}^{\pm}. This stability inequality interprets that changes in vectorizations are bounded by changes in persistence diagrams. Essentially, two nearby persistence diagrams correspond to nearby vectorizations. If a particular vectorization φ\varphi satisfy such a stability condition, we call them stable vectorization [3]. Notable examples of stable vectorizations include Persistence Landscapes [10], Silhouettes [18], Persistence Images [1], Stabilized Betti Curves [45], and various Persistence curves [20].

A.2 Stability of MultiPersistence Vectorizations

In this paper, because of technical problems in defining a multipersistence output like persistence diagrams (Appendix B), we directly moved the vectorization of the multifiltrations by a well-known method called slicing. In particular, assuming we have 2-parameter filtration {𝒳i,j}\{\mathcal{X}_{i,j}\}, in the multipersistence grid 𝒢\mathcal{G} of size m×nm\times n, for each fixed i0i_{0}, we get single filtration 𝒳^i0\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i_{0}}, 𝒳i0​1⊂𝒳i0​2⊂⋯⊂𝒳i0​n=𝒳i0\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}1}\subset\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}2}\subset\dots\subset\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}n}=\mathcal{X}_{i_{0}}, which can be considered as horizontal slicing of the multipersistence grid. Then, applying vectorizations above to the single filtrations {𝒳^i}1m\{\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i}\}_{1}^{m}, we get mm separate vectors φ→i=φ⁡(PD⁡(𝒳^i))\vec{\varphi}_{i}=\varphi(\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i})). Then, collecting these vectors into a 2-tensor as rows, we obtain a 2-tensor ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi} which we call the induced MP vectorization of φ\varphi. For example, when φ\varphi is Betti vectorization, ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi} is simply correspond to multigraded Betti numbers [61], which are simply m×nm\times n matrices for each Betti dimension. We now show that when the source single parameter (SP) vectorization φ\varphi is stable, then so is its induced MP vectorization ℳφ\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}.

Let 𝒳+\mathcal{X}^{+} and 𝒳−\mathcal{X}^{-} be two images of size r×sr\times s. With the notation in Section A.1, let φ\varphi be a stable SP vectorization with the stability equation

d⁡(φ⁡(𝒳+),φ⁡(𝒳−))≤Cφ⋅𝒲pφ​(PD⁡(𝒳+),PD⁡(𝒳−))\mathrm{d}(\varphi(\mathcal{X}^{+}),\varphi(\mathcal{X}^{-}))\leq C_{\varphi}\cdot\mathcal{W}_{p_{\varphi}}(\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{+}),\mathrm{PD}(\mathcal{X}^{-}))

 (21)

for some 1≤pφ≤∞1\leq p_{\varphi}\leq\infty. Note that for many common stable vectorization φ\varphi, d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is taken as lpφl^{p_{\varphi}} metric [71]. However, to keep the generality, we are not specifying it here.

Now, we consider the define these multiple single persistence diagrams {PD⁡(𝒳^i±)}\{\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i}^{\pm})\} as output for the multipersistence grid, and define a natural matching distance between as the sum of the corresponding distances for each row.

𝐃p​({PD⁡(𝒳^i+)},{PD⁡(𝒳^i−)})=∑i=1m𝒲p​(PD⁡(𝒳^i+),PD⁡(𝒳^i−)).\resizebox{27677874}{}{$\mathbf{D}_{p}(\{\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i}^{+})\},\{\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}_{i}^{-})\})\\ =\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{W}_{p}(\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{+}_{i}),\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{-}_{i}))$}. (22)

Now, we define the distance between induced MP vectorizations as

𝔇⁡(ℳφ​(𝒳+),ℳφ​(𝒳−))=∑i=1md⁡(φ⁡(𝒳i+),φ⁡(𝒳i−))\mathfrak{D}(\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}(\mathcal{X}^{+}),\mathcal{M}_{\varphi}(\mathcal{X}^{-}))=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{d}(\varphi(\mathcal{X}^{+}_{i}),\varphi(\mathcal{X}^{-}_{i})) (23)

where p≥1p\geq 1.

Corollary 2 (CumPerLay is stable).

Let ΨMP\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}} represent CumPerLay vectorization as defined in Section 4.1. Let 𝒦\mathcal{K} be a cubical complex and let F,G:𝒦→ℝ2F,G:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}^{2} be bifiltration functions. Let 𝒦^F,𝒦^G\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F},\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{G} be the induced bipersistence modules. Then, we have

𝔇⁡(ΨMP​(𝒦^F),ΨMP​(𝒦^G))≤C^ΨMP​‖F−G‖∞\mathfrak{D}(\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}),\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{G}))\leq\widehat{C}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}}\|F-G\|_{\infty}
Proof.

The proof follows from the stability of Perslay Vectorizations [15], and the previous stability theorem. In particular, while the authors proved their stability theorem for clique complexes in [15], their proofs as single persistence vectorization extends to cubical complexes as all the relevant results extends to this context [71]. By [14, Theorem A.2], as single persistence module, for each row 1≤m0≤M1\leq m_{0}\leq M of the bipersistence module 𝒦^\widehat{\mathcal{K}}, we obtain dB​(PD⁡(𝒦^Fm0),PD⁡(𝒦^Fm0)≤‖F−G‖∞CLOSEd_{B}(\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}^{m_{0}}),\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}^{m_{0}})\leq\|F-G\|_{\infty} where 𝒦^m0\widehat{\mathcal{K}}^{m_{0}} represents m0t​hm_{0}^{th} row in bipersistence module 𝒦^\widehat{\mathcal{K}}. As Perslay vectorizations are stable, we obtain

d⁡(ΨMPm0​(𝒦^F),ΨMPm0​(𝒦^F)≤Cm0​dB​(PD⁡(𝒦^Fm0),PD⁡(𝒦^Fm0)CLOSECLOSE\mathrm{d}(\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}^{m_{0}}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}),\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}^{m_{0}}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F})\leq C_{m_{0}}d_{B}(\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}^{m_{0}}),\mathrm{PD}(\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{F}^{m_{0}})

where ΨMPm0\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}^{m_{0}} represents restriction of ΨMP\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}} to m0t​hm_{0}^{th} row. After obtaining similar inequality for each row, the proof follows by following the same procedure in the proof of Thm. 1 where C^ΨMP=∑m=1MCm\widehat{C}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{MP}}}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}C_{m}. ∎

While we define the metrics and MP vectorizations for a 2-parameter case, it can naturally be adapted to any multiparameter case. Similarly, the proof can easily be adapted to higher dimensional images. In this paper, we utilize Silhouette and Betti curves as the vectorization method φ\varphi. while Betti curves are not stable with respect to the bottleneck (𝒲∞\mathcal{W}_{\infty}) distance [2], they are stable with respect to the 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}-metric [31]. On the other hand, Silhouette vectorizations are stable as they are derived from persistence landscapes [11, 18]. Therefore, by applying Thm. 1 to these vectorizations, we have the stability for both MP Betti and MP Silhouette vectorizations, we employed in this paper. Furthermore, adapting the stability result given in [61] to our setting, one can obtain another proof for the stability of MP Betti vectorization with respect to a signed Wasserstein-1 distance, a bottleneck-type metric they introduce.

Appendix B Multiparameter Persistence Theory

Multipersistence theory has garnered significant research interest due to its potential to enhance the performance and robustness of single persistence theory. While single persistence extracts topological features from a one-parameter filtration, a multidimensional filtration with multiple parameters should, in principle, provide a richer and more informative summary for machine learning applications. However, technical challenges in the theory have hindered its full realization, leaving multipersistence largely unexplored in the ML community. Here, we summarize these key challenges. For a more detailed discussion, [9] provides an overview of the current state of the theory and its major obstacles.

In single persistence, the threshold space {αi}\{\alpha_{i}\} is a totally ordered subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}, meaning that any topological feature appearing in the filtration sequence {Δi}\{\Delta_{i}\} has a well-defined birth and death time, with birth occurring before death. This ordering property allows for the decomposition of the persistence module M={Hk​(Δi)}i=1NM=\{H_{k}(\Delta_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} into barcodes, a concept formalized in the 1950s through the Krull-Schmidt-Azumaya Theorem [9] (Theorem 4.2). This decomposition forms the basis of what is known as a Persistence Diagram.

However, in higher dimensions (d=2d=2 or more), the threshold set {(αi,βj)}\{(\alpha_{i},\beta_{j})\} is only partially ordered (a poset), meaning that while some indices have a clear ordering (e.g., (1,2)<(4,7)(1,2)<(4,7)), others do not (e.g., (2,3)(2,3) vs. (1,5)(1,5)). Consequently, in a multipersistence grid {Δi​j}\{\Delta_{ij}\}, birth and death times are no longer well-defined. Furthermore, the Krull-Schmidt-Azumaya Theorem does not extend to higher dimensions [9] (Section 4.2), making barcode decomposition impossible for general multipersistence modules. This fundamental limitation prevents a straightforward generalization of single persistence to multipersistence. Even in cases where a meaningful barcode decomposition exists, the challenge remains of faithfully representing these barcodes due to the inherent partial ordering. Multipersistence modules are an active area of research in commutative algebra, with further details available in [33].

Despite these challenges, several approaches have been proposed to leverage the multipersistence framework [52]. One of the earliest methods, introduced by [53], involves analyzing one-dimensional slices of the multipersistence grid to extract the most dominant features. Later, [14] expanded this idea by considering multiple slicing directions (vineyards) and summarizing multiple persistence diagrams (PDs) into a vectorized representation. These slicing-based techniques extract persistence diagrams from predetermined one-dimensional slices and aggregate them into a lower-dimensional summary [9]. However, this approach presents two major issues: (1) the topological summary heavily depends on the chosen slicing directions, making direction selection a nontrivial problem, and (2) compression of information from multiple persistence diagrams may lead to significant information loss.

A different approach to vectorizing multipersistence modules was introduced by Vipond [77], who extended persistence landscapes into higher dimensions. Unlike slicing-based methods, this approach does not rely on a predetermined global slice direction. Instead, for each point 𝐱∈ℝn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, where nn is the dimension of the multipersistence module, the kthk^{\text{th}}-landscape explores the widest direction in which the rank invariant has a nontrivial image. From this perspective, the Multipersistence Landscape can be seen as a more faithful representation of the multipersistence module. While this method is particularly effective in settings where key insights come from a few dominant topological features (e.g., point clouds or sparse data), its computational complexity limits its practicality for large datasets with many topological features. Recently, [17] introduced the meta-rank and meta-diagram as novel invariants for 2-parameter persistence modules, demonstrating their equivalence to the rank invariant and signed barcode while providing computational improvements and an intuitive visualization as a persistence diagram of diagrams. Again, very recently, [56] extends stable vectorization techniques from one-parameter to multiparameter persistent homology by leveraging signed barcodes as signed Radon measures, enabling the computation of informative and provably stable feature vectors that enhance performance in topology-based data analysis.

While these approaches effectively capture dominant topological patterns in sparse data, their applications are largely limited to point cloud and graph settings. In contrast, our approach offers a more computationally efficient and versatile vectorization for cubical multipersistence, where the key topological signatures mostly arise from tracking the density of small features, making it suitable for image analysis.

Appendix C Common Multifiltrations for Images

There are several natural multifiltration methods for cubical persistence the images offer. Here, we list some of them.

Bifiltrations on binary images

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be an image of size r×sr\times s. A bifiltration induced from 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a collection of binary images {𝒳m,n}\{\mathcal{X}_{m,n}\} of the same size where 𝒳m,n⊂𝒳m+1,n\mathcal{X}_{m,n}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m+1,n} and 𝒳m,n⊂𝒳m,n+1\mathcal{X}_{m,n}\subset\mathcal{X}_{m,n+1} for any 1≤m≤M1\leq m\leq M and 1≤n≤N1\leq n\leq N. In other words, a bifiltration defines a grid 𝒢\mathcal{G} of size M×NM\times N where each individual row and column represents a regular filtration as shown in Fig. 9, i.e., for any fixed 1≤m0≤M1\leq m_{0}\leq M (row), the sequence {𝒳m0,n}1N\{\mathcal{X}_{m_{0},n}\}_{1}^{N} is a regular filtration of length NN (column), and for any fixed 1≤n0≤N1\leq n_{0}\leq N, the sequence {𝒳m,n0}1M\{\mathcal{X}_{m,n_{0}}\}_{1}^{M} is a regular filtration of length MM.

Color multifiltrations.

The primary objective of multiparameter persistence lies in effectively leveraging multiple parameters, especially when data offers more than one function to utilize. In color images, each image inherently comprises three natural functions, denoted as RR, GG, and BB. Thus, for every pixel Δi​j\Delta_{ij}, there exist corresponding color values: Ri​j,Gi​j,Bi​j∈[0,255]R_{ij},G_{ij},B_{ij}\in[0,255]. To proceed, we establish a three-parameter multifiltration with parameters {sm}1N1\{s_{m}\}_{1}^{N_{1}}, {tn}1N2\{t_{n}\}_{1}^{N_{2}}, {vr}1N3\{v_{r}\}_{1}^{N_{3}}, where sm,tn,vr∈[0,255]s_{m},t_{n},v_{r}\in[0,255] are threshold values for color channels R,GR,G, and BB respectively. By simply defining binary images 𝒳m,n,r={Δi​j⊂𝒳∣Ri​j≤sm,Gi​j≤tn,Bi​j≤vr}\mathcal{X}_{m,n,r}=\{\Delta_{ij}\subset\mathcal{X}\mid R_{ij}\leq s_{m},G_{ij}\leq t_{n},B_{ij}\leq v_{r}\}, we induce a three-parameter multipersistence module {Hk​(𝒳m,n,r)}\{H_{k}(\mathcal{X}_{m,n,r})\}, yielding Betti tensors 𝐁k​(𝒳)=[βm,n,rk]\mathbf{B}_{k}(\mathcal{X})=[\beta^{k}_{m,n,r}]. These tensors constitute 3​D3D arrays with dimensions N1×N2×N2N_{1}\times N_{2}\times N_{2} (See Fig. 3).

Erosion bifiltrations.

One significant limitation of sublevel filtration is its inability to provide information about the sizes of topological features. Instead, it only focuses on the difference in function values between when a topological feature is born and when it dies. To illustrate, consider a grayscale image where all pixels have a grayscale value of 00 except for one pixel in the center with a value of 255255. The resulting persistence diagram would feature a single large bar [0,255)[0,255), indicating a very small topological feature—a hole with a diameter of 11. Conversely, a binary image in 𝒳100\mathcal{X}_{100} might contain a large hole with a diameter of 20, where the pixels of the hole have color values between 101 and 105, then it will be completely filled in by 𝒳105\mathcal{X}_{105}. Despite the significant change in the hole’s size, the grayscale sublevel filtration would only yield a small bar (100,105)(100,105) reflecting the difference in grayscale values (color contrast of the hole), without conveying any information about the hole’s size.

While persistence homology aims to identify the topological features present in a filtration, sublevel filtrations cannot inherently capture size information for these features. However, alternative filtration methods such as erosion, dilation, and signed distance filtrations have been proposed to address this issue [36]. These methods offer avenues to incorporate size information into the analysis of topological features, complementing the capabilities of sublevel filtration.

To capture topological features created by the images as well as their sizes, a natural approach is to combine grayscale sublevel filtration with erosion filtration. Erosion filtration is defined for binary images, and basically, it is a sublevel filtration for a special function, called erosion. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a grayscale image of size r×sr\times s, and let {𝒳m}1M\{\mathcal{X}_{m}\}_{1}^{M} be the sublevel filtration induced by grayscale values described in Section 3. Each 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} is a binary image with some topological features. Let Ωm\Omega_{m} represent all black pixels in 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is r×sr\times s grid. Then, for each 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m}, we define an erosion function ξm:𝒢→𝒩\xi_{m}:\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{N} such that ξm​(i,j)=𝒟⁡(Ωm,Δi​j)\xi_{m}(i,j)=\mathcal{D}(\Omega_{m},\Delta_{ij}) where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the Manhattan (L1L_{1}) metric between the pixel Δi​j\Delta_{ij} and the black region Ωm\Omega_{m}. In other words, ξm​(i0,j0)=inf{|i0−i′|+|j0−j′|∣Δi′​j′⊂Ωm}\xi_{m}(i_{0},j_{0})=\inf\{|i_{0}-i^{\prime}|+|j_{0}-j^{\prime}|\mid\Delta_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\subset\Omega_{m}\}. In particular, for each Δi​j∈Ωm\Delta_{ij}\in\Omega_{m}, ξm​(i,j)=0\xi_{m}(i,j)=0. Intuitively, erosion function ξm\xi_{m} gives 00 values to all black pixels in the binary image 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m}, and measures the L1L_{1} distance of each white pixel to black region Ωm\Omega_{m} in 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} (See Fig. 10). Then, for each mm, the bifiltration {𝒳m,n}\{\mathcal{X}_{m,n}\} is defined as the collection of binary images 𝒳m,n={Δi​j∈𝒳∣ξm​(i,j)<n}\mathcal{X}_{m,n}=\{\Delta_{ij}\in\mathcal{X}\mid\xi_{m}(i,j)<n\}. Hence, if there is a white hole in 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m}, the value dd of the farthest pixel in the hole to Ωm\Omega_{m} measures the radius of the whole, and produces a bar of size [0,d)[0,d) in the persistence diagram. In a way, erosion filtration is enabling to measure the size of the wholes in binary images. Recall that the persistence bars for sublevel filtration for color values only give the color difference (contrast) of the hole independent of the size of the hole. Therefore, color filtration and erosion filtration are completely complementary to each other, and combining them produces a very powerful filtration model for the image. Signed distance and dilation are other types of filtrations to capture the size of the topological features in binary images, similar to erosion filtration [36].

Appendix D Implementation Details

In Algorithm 1, we present the main algorithm for our CUDA GPU implementation of Cubical Persistence and Cubical Multiparameter Persistence. The two main C++/CUDA functions are further explained in Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3. Our implementation is influenced by the CPU-based CubicalRipser software [47] for SP. We utilize the duality between top-dimensional cell and vertex constructions in persistent homology [7] to efficiently compute 0th and 1st dimensional homology of 2D images with only minor modifications to the algorithm. The compact multifiltration inputs (corresponding to NN MP filtration inputs with CC row-wise slices) are used to construct an input grid whose structure depends on the target dimension. For the 0th dimension, the compact filtration input is padded with a threshold value (a constant input representing infinity), corresponding to a primal grid. For the 1st dimension, the input values are padded with threshold, inverted, and then padded again, corresponding to an Alexander Duality-based dual grid. Following this, Algorithm 2 iterates over all edges (horizontal and vertical for both dimensions, plus diagonal edges for the 1st dimension), computes filtration values based on the compact filtration inputs in parallel over the batch, width, and height dimensions, and finally sorts the values in a descending order.

In Algorithm 3, we use a union-find-based algorithm with a CUDA-adapted implementation of Union-Find [74] with path compression and union by rank. The initialization of the union-find data structure is parallelized over each batch element and each pixel. The main loop, which calculates persistence pairs by iterating over edges sorted by decreasing death times, is parallelized only over the batch dimension. Since the number of persistence pairs can vary per input and is not known beforehand, we use a chunking mechanism. Based on a provided chunk size hyperparameter, the loop is executed until a maximum of chunk size pairs are generated for each batch element, while the number of persistence pairs is tracked separately. The kernel for this loop is executed iteratively until the computation for each batch element is complete. The resulting chunks are then concatenated and processed in parallel. This approach allows variable-length persistence pair outputs and can be further optimized by fine-tuning the chunk size hyperparameter for a given task.

Finally, we extract the final persistence pairs using the coordinate locations that correspond to the birth and death values in the original MP filtration. The algorithm’s output for variable-length persistence pairs consists of two tensors: a zero-padded tensor containing the persistence pairs for each batch element and row-wise slice, and a separate tensor storing the lengths for each batch element and row-wise slice. This output is then processed by our CuMPerLay vectorization layer, which takes masked persistence pair tensors as inputs. While we typically use a chunk size of 1024, this hyperparameter can be dynamically adjusted during training based on the maximum number of persistence pairs observed in recent batches.
